title: Urging Ontario to keep Guelph's consumption site open
subtitle: Council also opposed using the notwithstanding clause on encampments and backed the Solve the Crisis campaign.
overview: Council spent the morning on three motions about homelessness and addiction. It asked the Ontario government to let Guelph's consumption and treatment site keep operating past its planned March 2025 closure {{vote:m6}}, to maintain or expand funding for the proposed HART hubs {{vote:m7}}, and not to prohibit supervised consumption sites {{vote:m8}}.

Council also opposed use of the Notwithstanding Clause to override Charter rights in encampment relocations {{vote:m14}}. A second clause on involuntary treatment was withdrawn after a councillor questioned whether the mayors' request letter covered it, so Council took no position on it. Council then endorsed Ontario's Big City Mayors' Solve the Crisis campaign, including a call for a provincial task force that includes people with lived experience {{vote:m20}}.

As part of the consent report, Council approved a $448 thousand budget adjustment for paramedic facility renewal. The motions about the province are requests to other governments, so they do not change local services directly, but they set out Guelph's formal position.

decisions.detail: Council urged the Ontario government to keep permitting and funding Guelph's consumption and treatment site beyond the proposed March 2025 end date {{vote:m6}}.
Council encouraged the province to maintain, if not expand, funding for the proposed Homelessness and Addiction Recovery Treatment hubs {{vote:m7}}.
Council encouraged the province not to prohibit establishing supervised consumption sites, including urgent public health needs sites {{vote:m8}}.
Council opposed use of the Notwithstanding Clause, as requested by a group of Ontario mayors, to prevent courts ruling on Charter rights in encampment relocations {{vote:m14}}.
Council directed a letter to AMO, Ontario's Big City Mayors and the 12 other municipalities in the mayors' request letter explaining its opposition {{vote:m15}}.
Council asked the province to form a task force, including people with lived experience, to develop a Made in Ontario action plan and review successful local programs {{vote:m20}}.

Council supported the campaign's remaining asks, including making homelessness a health priority, a single responsible provincial ministry and sustainable funding from both senior governments {{vote:m21}}.
Council approved Q3 budget monitoring funding adjustments and a $448 thousand adjustment for paramedic facility renewal, passed with the consent report {{vote:m3}}.

debate: Delegates and several councillors argued the consumption site saves lives and costs, that the HART hubs do not replace harm reduction, and that closure will push more overdose response onto paramedics, hospitals and businesses.

A councillor proposed adding "at least until the HART hub is fully operational" to the site request to bridge a likely gap. Opponents said the hubs do not replicate a consumption site, so the gap would not end, and the amendment was defeated {{vote:m5}}.

On the Notwithstanding Clause, delegates said using it against encampments would override rights of the most marginalized people. Supporters said it lets the province avoid funding housing and mental health supports. The mayor said public spaces such as playgrounds must stay usable and noted the letter referred to use only if necessary.

The involuntary treatment clause drew questions about what "outside the existing process" meant and whether Council had enough expertise. Several councillors said they were not qualified to judge it, and it was withdrawn.

On Solve the Crisis, one councillor tried to remove the business and tourism sectors from the proposed task force and add people with lived experience. Others said all affected groups should be at the table, and the removal was defeated {{vote:m17}}. Two councillors objected to another provincial task force, saying delay is the risk and permanent housing funding is the need.
